title: Who Really Knows?
hookLine: the creation hymn says even the gods came later, and ends on a question. in hinduism, asking is part of the path
carry: in hinduism, asking is part of believing
tomorrow: a person with a thousand heads. who is he?

lines: WHERE WAS I BEFORE I WAS BORN?
A CONFIDENT ANSWER, OR A NEW SUBJECT?
OR: NOBODY HAS SEEN THAT FAR BACK.
cards: Where was I before I was born? A small child might ask it at bedtime, wide awake, while the grown-up in the doorway searches for an answer. There are a few ways to handle it.
Give a confident answer. Change the subject. Or sit on the edge of the bed and say, honestly, that's a big one, and nobody has seen all the way back.
The Nasadiya Sukta has circled a bigger version of that question since its first verse. In its last two, it asks it straight out.

teach.h: KO ADDHA VEDA: WHO REALLY KNOWS?
teach.b: Verse six opens with a question. Ko addha veda. Who really knows?
Who here could declare it, where this was born, where this creation came from? Then a startling line.

teach.h: THE GODS CAME AFTER THE MAKING.
teach.b: The gods, it says, came after this world's making. So even the gods weren't there to see the start. Who, then, knows where it arose?
Verse seven tries one more answer. Whether it was made or not, the one who watches over it in the highest heaven surely knows.

And then the hymn's last words: or perhaps that one does not know. So anga veda yadi va na veda. Some traditional readers hear reverence there: the beginning is so deep only the highest could know it.
Some modern readers hear honest doubt, kept inside scripture. And this is a big Hindu teaching, hiding in plain sight: asking is part of the path.
The Brahma Sutras, the classic summary of the Upanishads' teaching, open with one line: athato brahma jijnasa. Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman. Not now, believe.
Now, ask. Arjuna spends much of the Bhagavad Gita asking Krishna questions, and Krishna answers. So for many Hindus doubt isn't faith's enemy; it's how faith goes deeper.
If someone tells you religion is only answers and science is only questions, the Rig Veda's own creation hymn ends with a question mark, and it is still chanted.

how: Hindu commentators and modern readers hear the Nasadiya Sukta's closing 'or perhaps does not know' in different ways; the hymn is still kept in Vedic recitation, and inquiry (jijnasa) is honored as a path in Hindu teaching.

games.q: a teacher says religion is all answers, science is all questions. what does the Rig Veda's creation hymn actually do at the end?
o: names the maker and settles it
ends on a question: or perhaps that one does not know
tells the reader to stop wondering
games.why: it ends: so anga veda yadi va na veda, that one surely knows, or perhaps does not know. in Hindu teaching, asking is part of the path.

practice: Bring up one thing you know because you were there, a face, a kitchen, a street you walked, and silently call it seen; then something you only believe, or were told, or wonder about, and call it not seen, gently, with no judgment.
Go back and forth for a while, noticing that both can be held in the same quiet mind; if you pray, bring one not-seen to God as an honest question, the way Arjuna did.
